planting.note: Plant container divisions in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; give Autumn Light room to reach its full upright height before crowding it with neighboring perennials.

directions: Unlike variegated selections such as Morning Light, Autumn Light keeps solid narrow green blades all season, forming a tall, gently arching fountain of foliage that stays clean and upright without staking. In late summer, airy silvery-white plumes rise well above the leaves and gradually take on a pink-tinged cast before fading to beige as seed matures, remaining showy into winter. The real signature of this cultivar is its fall foliage change, when the blades shift to warm bronze tones that give the clump a glowing quality in low autumn sun, distinguishing it from cousins grown chiefly for summer variegation. Cut the dried clump back to a few inches in late winter before new growth emerges, and site it where afternoon light can catch the plumes and bronzed foliage for maximum effect.

common_name: Little Honey Dwarf Variegated Fountain Grass

planting.note: Plant container divisions in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Little Honey holds its white variegation best with consistent sun exposure and regular moisture through the first season.

directions: Little Honey arose as a white-centered sport discovered on the miniature cultivar 'Little Bunny,' and it keeps that same diminutive, tightly clumping stature while adding crisp white-and-green striped blades that set it apart from every solid-green dwarf fountain grass selection. The variegation brightens shaded corners of a sunny border and reads almost silvery in mass, especially against dark mulch or bronze-leaved companions. Soft, arching plumes in pale greenish-white appear in late summer just above the foliage, a subtler, more subdued flower display than larger alopecuroides cultivars produce. Because it stays so compact, Little Honey excels at the front of borders, in rock gardens, and in containers; shear the clump back to a few inches in late winter before new growth resumes.

planting.note: Plant container divisions in spring in average to moist, well-drained soil in full sun; China's fine foliage texture and tidy habit make it a good choice where a smaller-scaled maiden grass is needed.

directions: China stands out among maiden grass cultivars for its exceptionally fine, needle-narrow olive-green blades, giving the arching clump an especially soft, airy texture even by miscanthus standards. In early autumn it sends up slender panicles that open brownish-red and age through dusky pink to silver, a subtler color progression than the stark silver-white plumes of Silberfeder or the early reddish flush of Malepartus. Its comparatively compact, well-behaved clump and refined texture suit smaller gardens and mixed borders where oversized miscanthus selections would overwhelm the space. This selection earned the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit for its reliable garden performance; cut the dormant clump back hard in late winter before new shoots emerge.

planting.note: Plant container divisions in spring in fertile, evenly moist but well-drained soil in a sheltered spot with morning sun or light shade; Dark Horse develops its deepest bronze color with some direct light and consistent moisture.

directions: A New Zealand native sedge selection, Dark Horse forms a tidy, evergreen tuft of narrow, gently arching olive-green leaves that flush deep bronze-red, intensifying to near-black tones through cool fall and winter weather. In late summer and early autumn, thin upright to arching flower spikes emerge in a striking blackish-purple, a darker, more dramatic display than the coppery tones typical of Carex buchananii or Carex testacea. Its compact, well-mannered clumping habit and tolerance of part shade make it easy to slot into container plantings, rock gardens, or the front of a mixed border where its dark coloring can contrast against silver or chartreuse companions. Avoid soggy winter soil and hot, dry exposure, both of which stress this selection; light grooming to remove tattered leaves in spring keeps clumps looking their best.

planting.note: Plant container divisions in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; give Blondo ample room, since it builds into one of the larger-scale maiden grass mounds over a few seasons.

directions: Blondo builds into a large, dense mound of green foliage noticeably fuller than mid-sized miscanthus selections, and it is grown chiefly for its outsized late-season flower display. Tall plumes emerge in a warm blonde-tan shade rather than the silver-white or pink-blushed tones of most maiden grass cultivars, then age to a pale silver that persists strongly through the fall and well into winter, catching low light beautifully. Its substantial bulk and abundant, long-lasting plumes make it an effective specimen or screening grass where a big seasonal statement is wanted, though its size means it needs more room than compact selections like Adagio or Little Kitten. Cut the entire clump back to a few inches in late winter before new growth resumes to keep the dense mound from becoming congested.
sources: Plants to Grow (Paul Drobot Plant Database)
